about: The Virginia state legal backbone for starting a glass studio: a hot shop (gas-fired glass furnace, glory hole, annealing kilns, torches), cold-working (grinding, polishing with water slurries), classes for the public, and possibly a cafe or sip-and-blow events. For each topic: the Code of Virginia and Virginia Administrative Code sections that govern it (quoted verbatim from law.lis.virginia.gov), what the state fixes versus what the locality decides, deadlines, fees, forms, escalation routes and caveats. The local layer (zoning, BPOL rates, fire official, building department, health district) is left for the place files.

caveats: Occupancy classification is set by the 2021 IBC, which is incorporated by reference and not printed on law.lis.virginia.gov. From the model code (paraphrased, not quoted): a hot shop with furnaces is a factory industrial use (Group F-1 covers glass products); a gallery that sells is mercantile (Group M); classes for the public are usually Group B (training and skill development) unless the space seats 50 or more, when it is Group A-3; a cafe seating 50 or more is Group A-2. Which group applies, and whether the mix is handled as separated or non-separated mixed use (IBC § 508), is the building official's call. Not grounded in Virginia text beyond the under-50 rule quoted above.

Exhaust and combustion-air requirements for furnaces, glory holes and kilns come from the 2021 IMC (Chapter 5 exhaust systems, including Section 510 hazardous exhaust where applicable) and the 2021 IFGC for gas piping and appliance connection; neither is reproduced on law.lis.virginia.gov. Only the state amendments in 13VAC5-63-310 were read, and they do not mention furnaces or kilns.

A listed furnace or glory hole is rare; most studio equipment is custom-built. Approval of unlisted equipment is at the building official's discretion under the IMC and IFGC rules for unlisted appliances (model-code paraphrase, not grounded in Virginia text).
Zoning is checked first: the building official cannot issue a certificate of occupancy for a use the zoning ordinance does not allow. See topic signs_hours_noise for the enabling law.

caveats: Liability waivers are not law. No Virginia statute or regulation read here requires, authorises or validates a waiver for students or event guests, and nothing in the permit process asks for one. Whether a signed waiver is enforceable is a matter of Virginia case law on exculpatory agreements, which is outside this file. A waiver never replaces the certificate of occupancy, the fire permits or insurance.

Minors as students (not employees) are not covered by the child-labour chapter, which regulates employment; the only section read that reaches a class instructor is § 40.1-103 (custody of a child, endangerment). No Virginia text sets a minimum age for a glassblowing student; that is a studio and insurer decision.

Minors as employees or interns: no federal or Virginia hazardous-occupation order read here names glass furnaces by name; 29 CFR Part 570 orders cover power-driven machines and some hot-work settings, and § 40.1-100.1 bars exposure to any recognized serious hazard. The 16VAC15-50 hazardous-occupations chapter read this run is the agricultural list and does not apply. Treat a hot shop as off-limits to employed minors unless DOLI says otherwise (inference).
Heat: there is no Virginia heat standard in force today; DOLI is developing one for adoption by May 1, 2028. Until then the general duty clause and the federal standards apply.
